7 nurses of color who made history
Nurses have long been credited as the backbone of the medical industry.
Without nurses, their expertise, their patient support, the day-to-day advocating, and the emotional and physical labor they expend, our health care system would stand still.
Despite the hard work of many, nurses from marginalized populations have consistently received the short end of the proverbial stick within health care—whether as employees, students, or patients.

As students, nurses of color experience a health care education fraught with implicit racial bias. According to a 2021 review by the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, health care students of color reported receiving less peer support, experiencing racial discrimination, and overall having "negative learning environments." Unfortunately, that experience often does not end once they complete their degree.
The health care system in the U.S. has a long way to go to reverse its ingrained structural racism. While racist policies have changed over time, health care disparities among marginalized populations continue to prevail and remain mistreated or undertreated, partly due to the lack of health care workers of color. Just 1 in 5 registered nurses identify as Asian, Black, or Hispanic, according to the 2020 National Nursing Workforce Survey.
As these disparities can also be connected to the ongoing effects of systemic racism and the historical neglect and mistreatment of patients of color, patient advocacy has long been a vital part of the nurse of color's job.
Many nurses of color throughout history have provided positive representation by making cultural competency, improved conditions, and medical advancements for communities of color their mission and life's work. Though Indigenous people in the U.S. have health care practices that predate modern nursing—many of which became the backbone for it—their contributions to the field are overlooked, along with those of other nurses of color.
Incredible Health offered a snapshot into the centuries of work that has been (and continues to be) done by highlighting seven nurses of color who have made history, drawing information from the American Society of Registered Nurses, Chamberlain University, the National Association of Hispanic Nurses, and other sources.

1. Mary Eliza Mahoney
Born in 1845, Mary Eliza Mahoney was the first Black woman to receive licensure as a nurse.
Starting in her teens, Mahoney held various jobs at the New England Hospital for Women and Children for 15 years. One of her roles was as a nurse's aide, leading her to learn about the profession before attending nursing school.

Prioritize a three-year infrastructure plan that changes who gets into nursing, who advances, how racism is addressed, and what leaders are held responsible for—not a standalone training event. In year one, establish a paid DEI implementation team with nurse-of-color representation, a protected budget line, executive sponsorship, and authority to change hiring, promotion, reporting, education, and scheduling practices. Make the chief nursing officer and each nursing leader accountable for a small public scorecard, reviewed quarterly, rather than making the DEI council solely responsible for progress. For the school pipeline, choose one or two nearby nursing programs, high schools, community organizations, or minority-serving institutions for sustained partnerships instead of scattering small grants across many groups. Fund the barriers that most affect persistence—application assistance, tutoring, mentoring, financial support, emotional support, advising, clinical exposure, and professional socialization—and continue the partnership through graduation and employment. Use paid nurse mentors and hospital-sponsored clinical experiences, with clear conversion goals for internships, graduate nurse positions, and two-year retention, because recruitment that ends at admission does not create a reliable workforce pipeline. For hiring, standardize job criteria, structured interviews, diverse interview panels, consistent reference checks, and documented reasons for selection, and audit each stage for racial disparities in applicant progression, offers, starting pay, specialty placement, and shift access. For promotion, publish transparent criteria, advertise opportunities broadly, use calibrated promotion panels, track time-in-role and advancement by race and level, and provide sponsorship—not only optional mentoring—for nurses of color seeking charge, educator, specialty, and management roles. Treat leadership development as a retention intervention by creating a nurse leadership academy with executive mentors, protected development time, stretch assignments, and succession planning for underrepresented nurses. Do not assume that increasing hiring will solve retention if nurses of color remain concentrated in less desirable shifts or excluded from specialty areas, professional opportunities, credit for ideas, and advancement. Build a reporting system that permits anonymous or confidential reporting, offers multiple routes outside the immediate chain of command, prohibits retaliation, provides rapid support, and tells the reporter what action was taken without compromising privacy. Include patient and visitor racism, peer harassment, manager misconduct, bullying, discrimination, and biased assignments in the same system, with severity definitions, response-time standards, independent review, and escalation to nursing and human-resources leadership. A low number of reports should not be treated as success, because nurses may avoid formal channels when they expect inaction or retaliation; measure reporting confidence, response satisfaction, repeat incidents, resolution time, and retaliation claims alongside report volume. Leaders should be required to intervene when patients request a nurse of a different race, use slurs, or otherwise target a nurse, while protecting the nurse rather than treating reassignment as the default solution. Make managers responsible for team climate through goals tied to fair scheduling, psychological safety, belonging, respectful conduct, equitable development access, retention gaps, and completion of corrective actions. Use continuing education to teach practical responses to racism, bystander intervention, structural racism, implicit bias, social determinants of health, and culturally safe care, and require managers to practice applying those skills to real workplace scenarios. Replace one-time mandatory training with a short foundational session, repeated microlearning, facilitated team discussions, manager coaching, and case review over many months; one evaluated program used an initial hour followed by 20 weeks of microlearning and frontline-leader conversations. Review the prelicensure curriculum and hospital orientation for hidden assumptions, curricular microaggressions, missing Black and other marginalized scholarship, and clinical examples that normalize racial inequity, using students and nurses of color as compensated co-designers rather than symbolic reviewers. The central tradeoff is breadth versus credibility: a smaller number of fully resourced commitments with visible follow-through will usually build more trust than a long list of unfunded promises. A second tradeoff is transparency versus confidentiality, so publish aggregate trends and action status while protecting identities and avoiding small-cell reporting that could expose individual nurses. A third tradeoff is treating representation as the goal versus treating it as an intermediate measure, so pair hiring and promotion targets with workload, belonging, psychological safety, compensation, specialty access, and retention outcomes. Prioritize a three-year infrastructure plan that changes who gets into nursing, who advances, how racism is addressed, and what leaders are held responsible for—not a standalone training event. [shard_04391_17236] [shard_01150_4330]

In year one, establish a paid DEI implementation team with nurse-of-color representation, a protected budget line, executive sponsorship, and authority to change hiring, promotion, reporting, education, and scheduling practices. [shard_04391_17236]

Make the chief nursing officer and each nursing leader accountable for a small public scorecard, reviewed quarterly, rather than making the DEI council solely responsible for progress. [shard_01150_4330] [shard_02368_44083]

For the school pipeline, choose one or two nearby nursing programs, high schools, community organizations, or minority-serving institutions for sustained partnerships instead of scattering small grants across many groups. [shard_04673_6562] [shard_02957_32488]

Fund the barriers that most affect persistence—application assistance, tutoring, mentoring, financial support, emotional support, advising, clinical exposure, and professional socialization—and continue the partnership through graduation and employment. [shard_05317_82197] [shard_02957_32488]

Use paid nurse mentors and hospital-sponsored clinical experiences, with clear conversion goals for internships, graduate nurse positions, and two-year retention, because recruitment that ends at admission does not create a reliable workforce pipeline. [shard_04673_6562]

For hiring, standardize job criteria, structured interviews, diverse interview panels, consistent reference checks, and documented reasons for selection, and audit each stage for racial disparities in applicant progression, offers, starting pay, specialty placement, and shift access. [shard_04391_17236] [shard_01899_5775]

For promotion, publish transparent criteria, advertise opportunities broadly, use calibrated promotion panels, track time-in-role and advancement by race and level, and provide sponsorship—not only optional mentoring—for nurses of color seeking charge, educator, specialty, and management roles. [shard_06420_13826] [shard_05930_50833]

Treat leadership development as a retention intervention by creating a nurse leadership academy with executive mentors, protected development time, stretch assignments, and succession planning for underrepresented nurses. [shard_05930_50833]

Do not assume that increasing hiring will solve retention if nurses of color remain concentrated in less desirable shifts or excluded from specialty areas, professional opportunities, credit for ideas, and advancement. [shard_04391_17236]

Build a reporting system that permits anonymous or confidential reporting, offers multiple routes outside the immediate chain of command, prohibits retaliation, provides rapid support, and tells the reporter what action was taken without compromising privacy. [shard_02192_66506] [shard_01159_55781]

Include patient and visitor racism, peer harassment, manager misconduct, bullying, discrimination, and biased assignments in the same system, with severity definitions, response-time standards, independent review, and escalation to nursing and human-resources leadership. [shard_02192_66506]

A low number of reports should not be treated as success, because nurses may avoid formal channels when they expect inaction or retaliation; measure reporting confidence, response satisfaction, repeat incidents, resolution time, and retaliation claims alongside report volume. [shard_01159_55781] [shard_02368_44083]

Leaders should be required to intervene when patients request a nurse of a different race, use slurs, or otherwise target a nurse, while protecting the nurse rather than treating reassignment as the default solution. [shard_02192_66506] [shard_04391_17236]

Make managers responsible for team climate through goals tied to fair scheduling, psychological safety, belonging, respectful conduct, equitable development access, retention gaps, and completion of corrective actions. [shard_01899_5775] [shard_02368_44083]

Use continuing education to teach practical responses to racism, bystander intervention, structural racism, implicit bias, social determinants of health, and culturally safe care, and require managers to practice applying those skills to real workplace scenarios. [shard_06378_24070] [shard_01154_45022]

Replace one-time mandatory training with a short foundational session, repeated microlearning, facilitated team discussions, manager coaching, and case review over many months; one evaluated program used an initial hour followed by 20 weeks of microlearning and frontline-leader conversations. [shard_05918_34146]

Review the prelicensure curriculum and hospital orientation for hidden assumptions, curricular microaggressions, missing Black and other marginalized scholarship, and clinical examples that normalize racial inequity, using students and nurses of color as compensated co-designers rather than symbolic reviewers. [shard_06378_24070] [shard_01154_45022]

With limited money, fund implementation capacity, reporting safety, advancement pathways, and manager accountability before expanding branding, conferences, broad awareness campaigns, or large generic training contracts. [shard_04391_17236] [shard_01150_4330]

The central tradeoff is breadth versus credibility: a smaller number of fully resourced commitments with visible follow-through will usually build more trust than a long list of unfunded promises. [shard_04391_17236]

A second tradeoff is transparency versus confidentiality, so publish aggregate trends and action status while protecting identities and avoiding small-cell reporting that could expose individual nurses. [shard_01899_5775] [shard_02192_66506]

A third tradeoff is treating representation as the goal versus treating it as an intermediate measure, so pair hiring and promotion targets with workload, belonging, psychological safety, compensation, specialty access, and retention outcomes. [shard_01899_5775] [shard_02184_40172]

Establish a baseline in the first six months and report quarterly results disaggregated by race and ethnicity, job level, unit, shift, employment status, and intersectional identities where privacy permits. [shard_01899_5775] [shard_02368_44083]

The outcome dashboard should include diverse applicants, hires, starting pay, offers accepted, specialty placement, promotions, leadership representation, participation in mentorship and development, turnover, intent to leave, absence, engagement, belonging, psychological safety, burnout, and patient-care incidents involving racism. [shard_02184_40172] [shard_01899_5775] [shard_02368_44083]

For the reporting system, measure awareness of reporting routes, perceived safety, reports per 100 employees, response time, resolution quality, repeat incidents, retaliation, and whether nurses believe leadership acted fairly. [shard_01159_55781] [shard_02192_66506]

For education, measure not merely attendance or test scores but confidence, observed intervention behavior, manager follow-through, curriculum changes, and changes in team-climate and patient-experience indicators. [shard_05918_34146] [shard_06378_24070]

By year two, use the data to remove bottlenecks in hiring, specialty assignment, promotion, and reporting, and by year three, tie budget renewal and leader evaluations to sustained improvement rather than to completion of activities. [shard_02368_44083] [shard_04391_17236]

The plan will feel performative if the hospital celebrates heritage months while nurses still experience slurs, patient-requested reassignment, stolen credit, blocked advancement, unsafe reporting, or no visible consequences for leaders. [shard_04391_17236]

It will also feel performative if nurses of color are repeatedly asked to educate colleagues without pay or authority, if the council collects stories but cannot change policy, if leaders publish representation numbers without retention data, or if “zero tolerance” is announced without enforcement. [shard_02192_66506] [shard_01150_4330]

The credibility test is whether a nurse of color can see a safer reporting route, a fairer opportunity to advance, meaningful support after an incident, and a leader whose evaluation and budget are visibly tied to fixing the problem. [shard_01150_4330] [shard_04391_17236]
